Smith chapter (Birkbeck PDF) confirms motion-onset capture and attentional synchrony, and that complex shots gave less synchrony (Results, Alexander Nevsky). "One magnet per shot; two magnets break synchrony" is an editorial extrapolation, not a tested result. 🟡.

"Film ASL ≈4–5 s [Cutting 2011]" is in kmilo pacing-and-cuts.md §Shot length, but kmilo says "It is a reference, not a target" and next line says talking-head YouTube runs faster (2–5 s). Rule adds "don't cut much faster than this" — not in source and contradicted by it. Also conflicts with science_james_cutting.md figure (≈3.5 s per Smith citing Cutting).

Smith chapter p.~2: AToCC argues match-on-action uses motion onsets, BUT Smith himself writes such analyses "are observational and based on hypotheses ... derived from post-hoc analysis" and that a stronger test is still needed. The replicated result is gaze clustering in general, not match-on-action. The evidence_note claim "measured and replicated" is overstated -> 🟡.

n=24 / Red Balloon / situation-change mediation all confirmed (Methods "Participants"; Results). The "cut there feels invisible" claim is not tested in this paper (it did not measure cut noticeability). 🟡.

Automatic segmentation during passive viewing is confirmed. But the mechanism "a mid-event cut forces a model update / reads as a jolt" is not shown; the paper reports the opposite direction for cuts per se: "cuts in and of themselves were not associated with increases in segmentation" (Appendix, cut analysis). Keep as craft rule at 🟡/🟠, drop the 🟢 mechanism claim.

Eye-trace matching across cuts is AToCC theory; Smith states continuity analyses are observational/post-hoc. "Kai studies me replicated" applies to gaze clustering, not to eye-trace placement across cuts. 🟡.
